title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
notes:
Task and constraints: Merge two lists that are already sorted in non-decreasing order. Either list may be empty, and existing nodes should be linked into the result rather than copied.
Idea: Compare the current nodes, link the smaller one after a tail pointer, and advance only the list from which that node came. Attach the remaining suffix when one list ends.
Technique and why it applies: Because both remaining suffixes are sorted, the smaller current head is always the next node in the merged order.
Invariant: The result prefix is sorted and contains exactly the nodes already removed from the two input fronts; tail is its final node.
Edge cases: A dummy head simplifies the first append. If one list is empty initially, the other list is returned through the same suffix attachment.
Complexity: Time is O(m+n) because each node is linked once. Extra space is O(1) because no new data nodes are allocated.
complexity_reason: Each existing node is advanced and linked once; only pointers are stored.

title: Generate Parentheses
notes:
Task and constraints: Generate every well-formed arrangement of n pairs of parentheses, with n at most 8. A prefix may never contain more closing than opening parentheses, and the final string must use n of each.
Idea: Build the string one character at a time. Add an opening parenthesis while fewer than n have been used; add a closing parenthesis only when it would not exceed the number of opens.
Technique and why it applies: These prefix constraints prune invalid branches before they become full candidates, so recursion generates only valid strings.
Invariant: The path has no more closes than opens and never uses more than n opens; each complete path has exactly 2n characters.
Edge cases: n=1 yields one pair. A closing parenthesis is permitted only when close < open.
Complexity: Work is proportional to the number of valid outputs times their length. Output space is O(Cn * n), where Cn is the nth Catalan number.
space_complexity: O(Cn * n) for returned strings; O(n) path
complexity_reason: Each valid combination has length 2n and must be materialized in the output.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
notes:
Task and constraints: Merge up to 10,000 sorted linked lists, with at most 10,000 nodes in total. The output should reuse the input nodes and remain sorted.
Idea: Put each non-empty list head in a min-heap. Repeatedly remove the smallest node, append it to the output, and insert its successor if present.
Technique and why it applies: The smallest unmerged node must be among the current heads because every list is sorted. A heap selects that head efficiently.
Invariant: The output contains the smallest nodes already removed from the heap in sorted order, and the heap contains the head of every remaining non-empty suffix.
Edge cases: Empty input and lists containing empty heads return null. Python uses a serial counter to avoid comparing node objects when values tie.
Complexity: Time is O(N log k) for N total nodes and k lists. Extra space is O(k) for the heap, excluding output links.
complexity_reason: At most one node per list is in the heap; each node is pushed and popped once.

title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
notes:
Task and constraints: Swap each adjacent pair of nodes in a singly linked list without changing node values. Lists may be empty or have an odd number of nodes.
Idea: Use a dummy node before the head. For each pair, keep references to the first and second nodes, point the first to the node after the pair, point the second to the first, and connect the previous tail to the second.
Technique and why it applies: Pairwise pointer rewiring swaps node positions in constant space without copying values.
Invariant: The list before the current pair is already swapped correctly, and prev points to its last node.
Edge cases: If fewer than two nodes remain, stop and leave the suffix unchanged. The dummy node handles swapping the original head.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each pair is processed once. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each pair is rewired once with a fixed number of pointers.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def swapPairs(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        prev = dummy
        while prev.next and prev.next.next:
            first, second = prev.next, prev.next.next
            first.next = second.next
            second.next = first
            prev.next = second
            prev = first
        return dummy.next

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse linked-list nodes in groups of size k. A final group with fewer than k nodes must remain in its original order, and node values must not be modified.
Idea: Find the kth node after the group predecessor. If it does not exist, stop. Otherwise reverse links through that kth node, connect the reversed group to the remaining suffix, and continue from the old group head.
Technique and why it applies: Group boundaries let the algorithm reverse exactly k links at a time while preserving the partial tail.
Invariant: All groups before group_prev are reversed correctly, and group_prev points to the node immediately before the next unprocessed group.
Edge cases: k=1 leaves the list unchanged. If fewer than k nodes remain, do not reverse them.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each node is traversed and relinked a constant number of times. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each group boundary and node is traversed a constant number of times.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
notes:
Task and constraints: The array is sorted. Keep one copy of each value in-place, preserve the sorted order, and return the count of unique values. Only the prefix of that length is relevant.
Idea: Keep a write index for the next unique value. Scan the array and copy a value only when it differs from the last value written.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting guarantees equal values are adjacent, so one comparison detects whether a value has already been kept.
Invariant: The prefix before write contains exactly the distinct values seen so far in sorted order.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns one. The stated constraints have at least one element, but the loop also naturally handles empty input.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for one scan. Extra space is O(1) because changes happen in-place.
complexity_reason: A single pass writes unique values into the existing array.

title: Remove Element
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove every occurrence of val in-place and return the number of remaining elements. The order may change, and values after the returned prefix are ignored.
Idea: Scan values and write each value unequal to val at the next output position.
Technique and why it applies: The problem only requires the surviving prefix, so overwriting skipped values is sufficient; no resizing or auxiliary array is needed.
Invariant: The prefix before write contains exactly the non-val values seen so far, in their original relative order.
Edge cases: If every value equals val, return zero. If none equals val, the write index reaches the original length.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because every element is inspected once. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The array is filtered in place with one write pointer.

title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the first index where needle occurs in haystack, or -1 if it does not occur. The strings contain lowercase English letters and can each have length 10,000.
Idea: Check each possible start index and compare the substring-sized window with needle until a match is found.
Technique and why it applies: The direct scan is simple and bounded by the given lengths; built-in substring search also implements this standard operation.
Invariant: Every candidate start before the current index has already been checked and does not match the needle.
Edge cases: A needle longer than haystack cannot match. The first matching occurrence must be returned, not a later one.
Complexity: The direct method is O((n-m+1)m) worst-case, or O(nm). Extra space is O(1) when comparing characters directly.
space_complexity: O(m) for Python slice copies; O(1) for Java character scan
complexity_reason: Each candidate may compare up to m characters; Python creates a temporary slice.

title: Divide Two Integers
notes:
Task and constraints: Divide two signed 32-bit integers without multiplication, division, or modulo operators. Truncate toward zero and clamp the quotient to the signed 32-bit range.
Idea: Work with positive magnitudes stored in a wider type, then repeatedly subtract the largest power-of-two multiple of the divisor that fits into the remaining dividend.
Technique and why it applies: Left shifts double a divisor repeatedly, allowing quotient bits to be found in logarithmically many subtraction steps.
Invariant: The remaining dividend is non-negative and equals the original magnitude minus the multiples already accounted for in the quotient.
Edge cases: The minimum integer cannot be safely negated in a 32-bit variable, so use long in Java. The one overflow result, minimum divided by -1, clamps to maximum.
Complexity: Time is O(log^2 M) for repeated shifts and subtraction in this straightforward version. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each outer iteration removes a shifted divisor; the inner loop searches shift sizes.

title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
notes:
Task and constraints: Find all indices where a substring consists of every word exactly once in any order. All words have equal length, and the source string may contain 10,000 characters.
Idea: For each alignment modulo word length, slide a window in word-sized steps, count words, and shrink when a word is overrepresented.
Technique and why it applies: Equal word lengths let the string be tokenized into fixed-width chunks; a frequency map checks whether the current chunk multiset matches the required words.
Invariant: The window contains whole words only, and after shrinking, no word count exceeds its required frequency.
Edge cases: Duplicate words require counts rather than a set. Empty word lists produce no starting indices. Different alignments must all be checked.
Complexity: Time is O(n) average map work per alignment in the standard sliding-window analysis, with O(u) extra space for distinct words and current counts.
time_complexity: O(n) average per alignment, O(n·width) across alignments
space_complexity: O(u) map storage plus substring objects
complexity_reason: Each word-sized chunk enters and leaves the sliding window a bounded number of times per alignment.

title: Next Permutation
notes:
Task and constraints: Rearrange an integer array into the next lexicographically larger permutation. If it is already the largest permutation, wrap around to the smallest ascending permutation. Modify the array in place.
Idea: Find the rightmost increasing pivot, swap it with the rightmost larger successor, then reverse the suffix after the pivot.
Technique and why it applies: The suffix after the pivot is non-increasing, so it is the largest possible arrangement for that prefix. Reversing it after the minimal increase produces the next permutation.
Invariant: The suffix remains non-increasing until the pivot is found; the chosen successor is the smallest value greater than the pivot in that suffix.
Edge cases: A fully descending array has no pivot and becomes ascending. Duplicates are allowed, so use strict comparisons.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each scan and reversal is linear. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Pivot search, successor search, and suffix reversal are linear in-place scans.

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
approach_name: DP length ending at each index
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest contiguous well-formed parentheses substring. The input may be empty and has at most 30,000 parentheses.
Idea: Let dp[i] be the longest valid substring ending at index i. A closing parenthesis may pair with the immediately previous opening parenthesis, or extend a valid substring ending just before the matching opening parenthesis.
Technique and why it applies: The ending position determines the only possible new valid suffix, and prior DP values summarize already-computed valid blocks.
Invariant: dp[i] is the length of the longest valid parentheses substring whose final character is s[i].
Edge cases: An opening parenthesis always gives zero. Guard all computed indices before looking for a matching opening parenthesis.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each index performs constant work. Extra space is O(n) for the DP array.
complexity_reason: Each DP entry is computed once using a constant number of earlier entries.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Search a target in a rotated ascending array with distinct values and return its index or -1. The required runtime is logarithmic.
Idea: At each binary-search step, at least one half is sorted. Check whether target lies inside that half's value range; keep that half if it does, otherwise search the other half.
Technique and why it applies: Rotation breaks global order but leaves one side of every midpoint partition sorted, which is enough to eliminate half the remaining indices.
Invariant: If target exists, its index remains within the current inclusive search interval.
Edge cases: A one-element array and a rotation pivot at either end work with inclusive bounds. Return immediately on equality.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) because the interval is halved each iteration. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The search interval is halved at each iteration.

title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
notes:
Task and constraints: In a sorted array, return the first and last indices of target, or [-1,-1] if absent. The array can be empty and the required runtime is logarithmic.
Idea: Use one binary search to find the first index whose value is at least target and another to find the first index whose value is greater than target.
Technique and why it applies: Lower-bound searches find boundaries in a sorted array without scanning the full run of duplicates.
Invariant: Each search keeps the boundary position within its binary-search interval; after convergence, the left pointer is the first index satisfying its comparison.
Edge cases: If the lower bound is n or its value is not target, the target is absent. Empty input returns [-1,-1].
Complexity: Time is O(log n) for two searches. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Two binary searches use constant state and no auxiliary arrays.

title: Search Insert Position
notes:
Task and constraints: Given a sorted array of distinct integers, return target's index if present or the index where it should be inserted to preserve sorted order.
Idea: Binary-search for the first position whose value is greater than or equal to target.
Technique and why it applies: The insertion point is exactly the lower bound, so a standard half-open binary search finds it without shifting the array.
Invariant: The insertion point always lies in [left,right], and every index before left contains a value smaller than target.
Edge cases: Target may be smaller than every value or larger than every value, yielding index zero or nums.length.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) because each step halves the interval. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: A half-open binary search uses constant space and halves the interval.

title: Valid Sudoku
approach_name: Track row, column, and box digits
notes:
Task and constraints: Validate a fixed 9x9 partially filled Sudoku board. Filled digits must be unique within every row, every column, and each 3x3 box; empty cells are represented by a dot.
Idea: Maintain a set for each row, column, and box. For each filled cell, reject if its digit is already in any of the three corresponding sets, then insert it into all three.
Technique and why it applies: A duplicate is exactly a repeated digit in one of these scopes, and a box index can be computed from its row and column.
Invariant: After processing each cell, all stored row, column, and box sets contain no repeated digit among the cells visited so far.
Edge cases: Dots are ignored. A board may be valid without being solvable; this method checks only the stated constraints.
Complexity: Time is O(1) for a fixed 9x9 board (or O(r*c) generally). Space is O(1) for the fixed number of sets and digit values.
complexity_reason: Only 27 sets of at most nine digits are maintained.
code:
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def isValidSudoku(self, board: List[List[str]]) -> bool:
        rows = [set() for _ in range(9)]
        cols = [set() for _ in range(9)]
        boxes = [set() for _ in range(9)]
        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                value = board[r][c]
                if value == '.': continue
                box = (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3
                if value in rows[r] or value in cols[c] or value in boxes[box]: return False
                rows[r].add(value); cols[c].add(value); boxes[box].add(value)
        return True

title: Sudoku Solver
approach_name: Try legal digits with constraint sets
notes:
Task and constraints: Fill a 9x9 Sudoku board so every row, column, and 3x3 box contains each digit from 1 to 9 exactly once. The board must be modified in place and the puzzle has a unique solution.
Idea: Find an empty cell, try each digit not already present in its row, column, or box, recurse, and undo the choice if it leads to a dead end.
Technique and why it applies: Sudoku constraints prune invalid assignments immediately; backtracking explores only locally legal candidates until the board is complete.
Invariant: Every assigned digit respects all row, column, and box constraints, and failed branches restore the board to its prior state.

title: Sudoku Solver
approach_name: Try legal digits with constraint sets
notes:
Task and constraints: Fill a 9x9 Sudoku board so every row, column, and 3x3 box contains each digit from 1 to 9 exactly once. The board must be modified in place and the puzzle has a unique solution.
Idea: Find an empty cell, try each digit not already present in its row, column, or box, recurse, and undo the choice if it leads to a dead end.

title: Count and Say
notes:
Task and constraints: Return term n of a sequence starting with "1", where each next term describes consecutive equal digits in the previous term using count followed by digit. n is at most 30.
Idea: Starting from "1", scan each term into runs, append each run's length and digit, and repeat until reaching n.
Technique and why it applies: This is direct run-length encoding; every new term depends only on the previous term.
Invariant: At the start of each iteration, the current string is exactly the requested sequence term for that iteration number.
Edge cases: A single-character run emits "1" followed by that character. The initial term is "1" without any encoding pass.
Complexity: Time is proportional to the total length of all generated terms up to n. Extra space is proportional to the next term's length.

title: Combination Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Return unique combinations of distinct positive candidates that sum to target. A candidate may be used repeatedly, and the number of valid combinations is limited by the test data.
Idea: Sort candidates, recursively choose a candidate, and recurse from the same index so it can be reused. Stop exploring a branch when the candidate exceeds the remaining target.
Technique and why it applies: Positive values make the remaining target decrease on each choice, and nondecreasing indices prevent permutations of the same combination from being generated separately.
Invariant: The path is nondecreasing by candidate index and its sum plus remaining equals the original target.
Edge cases: A candidate equal to target forms a single-element answer. Positive candidate values ensure recursion cannot loop indefinitely.
Complexity: Time is output-sensitive and exponential in the worst case. Recursion depth is O(target/minCandidate), excluding returned combinations.
complexity_reason: Positive candidates reduce the remaining target and each valid combination is emitted once.

title: Combination Sum II
approach_name: Use each candidate once and skip duplicates
notes:
Task and constraints: Return unique combinations summing to target when each input candidate can be used at most once. Candidate values are positive, and duplicate values may occur in the input.
Idea: Sort candidates and backtrack using the next index after each choice. At each recursion depth, skip a value equal to the previous value so identical branches are not repeated.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting groups duplicates together; using i+1 prevents reuse, while same-depth duplicate skipping preserves unique value combinations.
Invariant: The path uses increasing indices, its sum does not exceed target, and duplicate first choices at the same depth are skipped.
Edge cases: Several identical candidates may be used if they occur at different indices. Stop a loop when a value exceeds the remaining target because later values are no smaller.
Complexity: Time is exponential in the worst case, bounded by subsets explored. Recursion space is O(n), excluding the output list.
complexity_reason: The recursion depth is at most the number of candidates and each index is used at most once.
